dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Effective help: Justice outcomes outrank lawyer supply
st.an: The source accepts that justice outcomes, rather than lawyer supply alone, should guide access-to-justice policy and materially strengthens that proposition by explaining lawyers’ effects through substantive and relational expertise. Its synthesis finds that, in the studied case types, much of lawyers’ advantage comes from navigating procedure and helping courts follow their own rules, supporting direct procedural reform while preserving the qualified value of representation.
qs: **The headline finding.** For the case types researched to date, substantive-law knowledge    "explains surprisingly little" of lawyers' advantage over unrepresented lay people; the advantage    concentrates where lawyers navigate procedures that are "relatively simple (to lawyers)" and    where relational expertise gets courts to follow their own rules.

Sandefur's own later gloss, in her held full-text 2019 Daedalus piece (sandefur-access-to-what-2019): "Resolving justice problems lawfully does not always require lawyers' assistance, as a growing body of evidence shows" — with this article cited in the supporting footnote (fn 10) as part of that body of evidence.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s work-redesign logic by decomposing lawyers’ advantage into different forms of expertise. Its finding that procedural navigation and relational expertise matter more than substantive-law knowledge in studied civil cases helps identify which work may be routinised and which remains dependent on professional interaction and institutional context, although it does not directly evaluate AI, verification or deployment models.
qs: For the types of cases researched to date, knowledge of substantive law explains surprisingly little of lawyers' advantage compared to lay people appearing unrepresented.
Instead, lawyers' impact is greatest when they assist in navigating relatively simple (to lawyers) procedures and where their relational expertise helps courts follow their own rules.

kp.k: Lawyers' contribution remains obscured by inconsistent prior research
kp.d: Sandefur identifies lawyers as gatekeepers of public justice institutions, particularly hearings and trials, while arguing that unclear theory and inconsistent research designs have impeded understanding of their contribution. The held material contains only the 2015 article's abstract and commentary reconstructing it, not the full study; it makes no claims about AI.
qs: Lawyers keep the gates of public justice institutions, particularly through their roles in formal procedures like hearings and trials.
Yet, it is not clear what lawyers do in such quintessentially legal settings: conclusions from past research are bedeviled by a lack of clear theory and inconsistencies in research design.

kp.k: Synthesis identifies consensus and variation in representation effects
kp.d: The study synthesises existing research on lawyers' impact on civil case outcomes using meta-analysis and nonparametric bounding. Sandefur reports that this combination identifies a domain of consensus about lawyers' effects and explores variation across studies. The held abstract supplies no study count, sample sizes, numerical effect estimates or research coverage dates.
qs: Conceptualizing litigation work in terms of professional expertise, I conduct a theoretically grounded synthesis of the findings of extant studies of lawyers' impact on civil case outcomes.

Using an innovative combination of statistical techniques—meta-analysis and nonparametric bounding—the present study transcends previous work to reveal a domain of consensus for lawyers' effect on case outcomes and to explore why this effect varies so greatly across past studies.

kp.k: Substantive legal knowledge explains little of lawyers' advantage
kp.d: Sandefur reports that knowledge of substantive law explains surprisingly little of lawyers' advantage over unrepresented lay people. This finding is expressly limited to the types of cases researched to date; it does not establish that substantive expertise is unimportant in every legal setting.
qs: For the types of cases researched to date, knowledge of substantive law explains surprisingly little of lawyers' advantage compared to lay people appearing unrepresented.

kp.k: Procedural navigation and relational expertise drive greatest impact
kp.d: The abstract locates lawyers' greatest impact in navigating procedures that are relatively simple from lawyers' perspective and in using relational expertise to help courts follow their own rules. It characterises relational expertise through this function rather than providing a fuller definition.
qs: Instead, lawyers' impact is greatest when they assist in navigating relatively simple (to lawyers) procedures and where their relational expertise helps courts follow their own rules.

kp.k: Expertise framework extends beyond the legal profession
kp.d: Sandefur proposes that the distinction between substantive and relational expertise generalises to other professions, where both may shape professional conduct and its consequences. This is a stated theoretical generalisation; the held abstract does not present separate evidence from other professions.
qs: Findings for law generalize to other professions, where substantive and relational expertise may shape the conduct and consequences of professional work.

kp.k: Later gloss questions universal need for lawyers' assistance
kp.d: The document separately quotes Sandefur's 2019 Daedalus article, which cites the 2015 study in footnote 10 as part of the evidence that lawful resolution of justice problems does not always require lawyers. This is a later interpretation, not wording from the 2015 abstract, and does not claim that lawyers are universally unnecessary.
qs: Resolving justice problems lawfully does not always require lawyers' assistance, as a growing body of evidence shows

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sandefur makes no claims or predictions about AI. Her claim concerns the sources of lawyers' advantage over unrepresented people in civil litigation: substantive-law knowledge explains relatively little, while procedural assistance and relational expertise contribute most in the settings identified.
pts.d: In this 2015 article, Sandefur reports that lawyers' impact is greatest where they navigate procedures that are relatively simple to lawyers and help courts follow their own rules. She also proposes that the distinction between substantive and relational expertise generalizes to other professions. These are findings and generalizations about professional expertise, not predictions about automation or evidence that AI can replace lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The stated evidence basis is a synthesis of existing studies of lawyers' effects on civil case outcomes, combining meta-analysis and nonparametric bounding.
pts.d: Sandefur describes a theoretically grounded synthesis intended to identify a domain of consensus and explain variation across earlier studies. Only the abstract is held: it supplies no study counts, effect sizes, case-type breakdowns, or fuller methodological details. The evidence concerns human representation, not AI performance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings are retrospective and expressly limited to case types researched by the time of the 2015 article; no future AI timeframe is given.
pts.d: The abstract does not assert that substantive knowledge contributes little in every legal matter. Its qualification is the case types covered by existing research, and its strongest-impact claim identifies settings involving procedural navigation and courts' adherence to their own rules. The abstract also acknowledges weaknesses and inconsistencies in the prior research literature.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are civil litigants, particularly unrepresented lay people, lawyers providing representation, and courts.
pts.d: The comparison concerns lawyers' contribution to civil case outcomes relative to people appearing without representation. Courts are implicated because part of lawyers' contribution is helping institutions follow their own rules. Other professions are mentioned as potential settings for the substantive/relational distinction, but the abstract identifies no specific occupations or measured effects outside law. It makes no claims about AI-driven staffing, pricing, or legal-market changes.
